extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and typesetters in book/journal publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and practical guidelines for preparing, submitting, setting, proofreading, and making up book- and article-length manuscripts (typography, headings, proofs, and shop practice). Intended to govern manuscript preparation, typesetting conventions, and proofroom procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Center the longest line and let the indentation be governed by that; if the longest line is disproportionate, use an average of the long lines to give a centered appearance. Where quotations from different poems vary slightly in line length, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines; in blank verse align lines of approximately equal length; align consecutive rhyming lines and indent alternate rhymes alike; indent disproportionately short lines more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are given showing centered stanzas, aligned blank verse, and indentation for rhyming patterns (e.g., indent lines 2 and 4 when rhymes alternate). Follow the scheme in similar arrangements; center the longest line or average long lines when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain paragraphs; use hanging indention selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' (first line indented, others flush) are preferable. Use a hanging indention (first line flush, others indented) to bring into relief the opening word(s), to emphasize a paragraph number, or when a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See section on hanging indention for examples. Use hanging indention sparingly for emphasis or where layout requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and leading conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary standard lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads between the lines is called leaded; without leads is called solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most books are set leaded. Use standard leads unless a project requires solid setting; note that line spacing affects readability and layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slugs (spacing slugs) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A slug is a strip of metal thicker than a lead, used in make-up of pages after headlines, etc.; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points (a nonpareil and a pica).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slugs where extra vertical space is required after headings or other elements; choose 6- or 12-point slugs as standard practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-head (headline) formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed equally distant from both margins; center-heads are usually set in capitals or small capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a center-head runs more than one line, use an inverted 'pyramid' form for two or three lines, or hanging indention for more than three lines. Examples provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-head formatting and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page or column; it may be set in a separate line (usually flush) or run in with the paragraph to which it belongs (the more common form). Side-heads are most frequently set in italics with only the first word and proper names capitalized; sometimes set in caps and small caps or bold-face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show side-heads set flush, run-in, and with various capitalizations—prefer run-in italics with sentence-style capitalization unless house style dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-in head definition and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut-in head is a head placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page, usually set in different type and generally placed under the first two lines of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cut-in heads to call out material within a column; set in a contrasting type and position them under the first two lines as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box-head for ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: A box-head is a head for a column in a ruled table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat box-heads as table headings and format consistently with table rules and captions (see table sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-head conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A running-head is a headline at the top of each page, usually giving the main title on the verso and the chapter or subdivision title on the recto. A good working rule is to set them in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than the text type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep running-heads concise and consistently sized; use roman or italic capitals two sizes down from text to avoid visual competition with page text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph types: plain vs hanging
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two kinds of paragraphs: plain (regular) paragraphs with first-line indent and others flush; hanging paragraphs with first line flush and the others indented (hanging indention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain paragraphs for standard text and hanging paragraphs where layout or typographic emphasis requires them; illustrate usage in make-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof types and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and distinctions among proof types: galley-proof (impression of type in a galley), page-proof (impression of type made up into page form), plate-proof or foundry-proof (proof taken immediately before an electrotype cast, with black border), fold proof (a galley-proof containing author's corrections), and revise (a new proof corrected from a marked proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand which proof stage you are working with—plate proofs normally used for modern printing; each proof type has different purposes and implications for corrections and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The arranging of type-lines into page form is called the make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make-up decisions affect pagination, line breaks, and hyphenation; coordinate with designers and printers to avoid repeated corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folio and folio placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A folio is a page-number; even numbers belong on the verso and odd numbers on the recto. A drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place folios consistently; follow house style for top vs bottom placement and alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-title (bastard title)
rubrics_metrics.description: A half-title or bastard title is the abbreviated title of a book placed on a separate page preceding the full title-page, or the title of a part or chapter preceding the part on a separate page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide copy for half-title pages with manuscripts as part of title-page materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype vs Linotype differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype: composing machine that casts characters separately via matrices; Linotype: composing machine that casts entire lines as slugs. Monotype allows easier substitution of figures; linotype requires resetting of whole lines when numbers change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of implications for corrections: linotype resetting makes certain changes (e.g., renumbering footnotes) expensive and disruptive; plan numbering and layout accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript submission physical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be typewritten (preferable) or in perfectly clear handwriting; sheets of uniform size (q^'Xii^' desirable); use only one side of paper; never roll manuscripts; place them flat in a box or envelope; do not fasten except by pins or clips (which can be removed); when fastening pieces use mucilage not pins; leave liberal top and left margins; number pages consecutively and indicate inserted/omitted pages (e.g., '4A', '4B'; '4, 4-7').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these practical rules to avoid lost slips and to give readers/printers room for directions and queries. Provide copy for title-pages, prefaces, tables of contents, and indexes with the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling inserts and additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserted pages should be clearly indicated (e.g., 'Insert A', 'Insert B') and placed after the sheets to which they belong; indicate insertion points on the original pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark exactly where to insert additions to avoid misplacement; use prescribed labels and margin notes like 'Here insert A'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and footnote marking in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated either by indenting first line or by a ¶ mark. Footnotes should be clearly designated (separate them by a rule or use different color ink); indicate the word in the text with a superior figure corresponding to the note; footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number footnotes consecutively through an article or by chapter. Remember linotype resetting implications: a change in one note number may require resetting whole lines; prefer monotype/hand-set practices when frequent renumbering is anticipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading: use standard marks and answer queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return proofs promptly. In marking proofs, use standard proofreaders' marks; do not adopt a personal system. Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays and errors arise from unanswered queries. Use the standard mark set (see proofreader's marks) to ensure compositor comprehension; do not invent marks that comp could misinterpret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid costly and plate corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that changes in type cost money — omission or addition of a word may necessitate resetting from that point onward and may involve repaging or injuring plates. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make manuscripts as perfect as possible before delivering to the printer. Make necessary alterations in the galley-proof stage to avoid plate corrections and extra expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return original manuscripts with proofs and retain marked sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Return the original manuscript with the galley-proof so the proofreader can refer to it; each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set to assist in calculating costs properly chargeable to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain continuity of marked materials through stages to track changes and costs; always include previous marked proofs when sending subsequent proof stages back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreader responsibilities and professional behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you were the author; be careful about proper names and figures; if copy is unclear, look it up or query the author; transfer manuscript queries to the proof; be discreet and avoid trivial criticisms; correct anything palpably wrong even if copy asserts otherwise; do not follow copy blindly; the proofreader is judge of correctness and must learn the Manual to correct violations without constant reference to authors or editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hide behind the copyholder; cultivate a 'personal equation' with authors/editors; prioritize accuracy over speed; in rush situations, state limitations and disclaim further responsibility; put your initial at the top of every galley read or revised to track who worked it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholder conduct and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading voice; small words are as essential as big ones; enunciate plural -s; regulate speed and do not guess at words; sit at right angles to the reader; give the reader a chance to make corrections; develop a system of signals for typographic features; do not waste time informing the proofreader about matters of style (they should know the rules); be careful in transferring marks; in sending proofs ensure everything is included and consult job ticket for recipient information; fasten pins at the top center and indicate envelope contents; return reference volumes to the file nightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient copyholding speeds proofreading and reduces errors. Use codes/signals for italics etc., avoid wasting time with style directions, and always include manuscript with proofs when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and learn the standard proofreader's marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt and use the standard proofreader's marks (e.g., cap, small capitals, lower-case, italic, roman, bold-face, delete, indent/make a new paragraph, insert space, close up, bad spacing, transpose, move left/right, depress, imperfect letter, shove down, straighten crooked line, restore words crossed out, print as a logotype, cut in words omitted, query to author).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create a personal mark system; use the standard set so compositors can act without confusion. A partial list of common marks is provided with definitions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering and formatting notes on linotype vs monotype
rubrics_metrics.description: On linotype, changing a single footnote number may necessitate resetting the whole first line of each succeeding note to the end of the series and the line in the text bearing the reference. On monotype or hand-set matter, changing a number amounts simply to substituting one figure for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using linotype, number footnotes with foresight (consecutive numbering through article or by chapter) to minimize resetting; prefer monotype/hand-setting for flexible renumbering.
